content: Cradle cap, also known as infantile or neonatal seborrheic dermatitis, is a skin condition characterized by yellowish, patchy, greasy, scaly, and crusty rashes that typically appear on the scalp of newborns. It is not usually itchy and does not seem to cause discomfort to the baby. This condition most commonly begins within the first three months of life. The rash is often noticeable around the ears, eyebrows, or eyelids, but it can also appear in other areas, where it is referred to as seborrheic dermatitis rather than cradle cap. In some countries, the term pityriasis capitis is used to describe cradle cap. It is an extremely common condition, affecting approximately half of all infants, with most cases being mild. Severe cases of cradle cap are rare. The exact cause of cradle cap is not well understood, but it is not due to infection, allergies, or poor hygiene. It is thought to be related to overactive sebaceous glands in the skin of newborns, possibly influenced by maternal hormones still present in the baby’s circulation. These glands produce a greasy substance that causes old skin cells to adhere to the scalp instead of drying and falling off. There may also be a connection with skin yeasts, such as Malassezia furfur (formerly known as Pityrosporum ovale). Some nutrition-focused practitioners have speculated that the condition could be linked to an immature digestive system in the baby, which may impair the absorption of biotin and other B-complex vitamins. Home remedies are generally suitable for mild cases of cradle cap. However, medical attention is recommended if the condition worsens, becomes red and irritated, spreads to other parts of the body, or if the baby develops a persistent diaper rash. Conditions such as fungal infections (e.g., tinea capitis) and scabies can mimic cradle cap, and in rare cases, cradle cap may be associated with immune disorders. If the baby exhibits other concerning symptoms (e.g., diarrhea), a doctor should be consulted. Cradle cap often resolves as the baby matures, but studies have shown that it can persist into toddlerhood and, less commonly, into later childhood. It may recur during adolescence and persist into adulthood. An Australian study found that about 15% of children previously diagnosed with cradle cap still had eczema 10 years later. In some cases, cradle cap may evolve into atopic dermatitis or, rarely, be misdiagnosed psoriasis. For treatment of cradle cap on the scalp, behind the ears, or on the eyebrows, a common recommendation is to apply vegetable or mineral oil to the affected area and allow it to soak in overnight or for a shorter period. However, this approach may conflict with the fact that Malassezia yeasts thrive in oily environments. The softened scales can then be gently removed using a soft brush, toothbrush, comb, or cloth. Care must be taken to avoid excessive force, as this can worsen the condition and lead to temporary hair loss. There is no scientific evidence supporting these recommendations. Another popular treatment involves applying petroleum jelly (e.g., Vaseline) overnight, which allows the softened scales to either fall off during the night or be brushed off in the morning. A paste made from baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) applied to the affected area for 10 minutes may also help lift the scales. There is significant disagreement regarding the use of shampoos. Some sources advise against frequent shampooing, while others recommend it. Mild baby shampoos are often suggested, but the term mild is not clearly defined. Many baby shampoos contain detergent surfactants, perfumes, and other potential irritants that can exacerbate eczema. Switching to a shampoo with minimal irritants is a prudent approach. Medicated shampoos containing sulfur, selenium, zinc pyrithione, or salicylic acid are generally not recommended for infants, as they can sting the eyes and may worsen the dermatitis. In stubborn cases, some doctors may recommend medicated shampoos, while others caution against their use in newborns due to concerns about systemic absorption. Dandruff shampoos often contain sodium lauryl sulfate, a known skin irritant. Steroid and tar preparations have been used but come with significant drawbacks. Immunomodulators such as tacrolimus (Protopic) and pimecrolimus (Elidel) are not approved for use in children under two years of age. Ketoconazole shampoos and creams are increasingly favored for moderate to severe cases of cradle cap. Research suggests that this antifungal medication is not absorbed into the bloodstream. However, ketoconazole shampoos currently contain several problematic irritants and allergens, so using a formulation prepared by a compounding pharmacy may be a better option. Several studies have reported rapid and complete resolution of cradle cap following the injection of biotin, either to the baby or the breastfeeding mother. In one study, injections of B-complex vitamins were also effective. Intravenous administration (rather than intramuscular) is recommended. Small amounts of oral biotin have not shown efficacy in more recent trials, leading some compendia to dismiss biotin supplementation as ineffective. However, this conclusion is incorrect. Oral supplementation with liquid biotin is favored by some physicians, but a well-designed study is needed to determine the effective dosage for oral supplementation or the impact of injected biotin/B-complex in a larger sample. Biotin is a very safe vitamin with no known toxicity and is worth trying. A Swedish study found good results from massaging the scalp with small amounts of borage oil twice daily. Other remedies, such as burdock or chamomile extracts, aloe gel, and tea tree oil (Melaleuca oil) shampoos, have also been tested in medical trials and found to be useful. However, tea tree oil and aloe can act as sensitizers, so any worsening of symptoms should prompt discontinuation of the remedy. For cradle cap affecting the eyelids, typical medical advice involves cleansing the area with diluted baby shampoo applied to a cotton swab. There is no consensus on the appropriate dilution, which ranges from a few drops in warm water to a 50/50 mixture. No studies have been conducted to evaluate the efficacy or safety of this treatment. It is worth noting the potential issues with baby shampoos mentioned earlier. In adults, a study comparing soap and baby shampoo to commercial eyelid scrubs found that patients strongly preferred not to use soap or shampoo on their eyelids. Baking soda (a teaspoon in a cup of boiled water) has also been recommended and is well-tolerated by adults. Washing with boiled warm water may also provide relief.
